transcript.text: Samsung RS68A8820S9/EU flashing 22E on the display and the fridge side isn't as cold as it should be. What does 22E mean and can I fix it?

On Samsung fridge freezers, 22E is a fridge fan error: the control board isn't detecting the fan that blows cold air round the fridge compartment spinning as it should. That fits the fridge not being cold enough, because without that airflow the cold doesn't reach the fridge properly. 1. Ice build-up around the fan. Frost grows on the cooling coil and around the fan until the blades can't turn. This is very common and often just needs a full defrost, though if it keeps coming back it points to a defrost problem (the defrost heater or its sensor, or an iced-up drain).
2. That's less common, and usually shows up as a silent fan even when there's no ice.
3. Restricted airflow, such as food pressed against the vents or a door not sealing, letting in moist air that freezes faster. So yes, there's a good chance you can fix it yourself, at least for now. 1. Listen for the fan. Open the fridge door and press the door switch in by hand. If you hear whirring, the fan has power and is turning. If it's silent, or you hear scraping or ticking, it's likely jammed by ice or the motor has failed.
2. Look for ice. Check the back wall and around the vents inside the fridge for frost or a sheet of ice. Visible ice points to cause 1.
3. Do a full manual defrost, which is the main fix for 22E. Move your food into cool boxes (or to a friend's), switch off and unplug the fridge, prop the doors open, and put towels on the floor and shelves to catch meltwater. Leave it for about 24 hours so hidden ice behind the panels melts completely. A hairdryer or fan heater speeds things up and can warp the plastic, so let it thaw naturally. Then plug it back in, let it cool for a few hours before reloading, and see whether 22E comes back.
4. While it's empty, check the door seals for splits or gaps, and make sure the vents won't be blocked when you reload. What the result tells you: if the code clears and it stays fine for weeks, it was a one-off ice-up. If 22E returns within days or a couple of weeks, the defrost system isn't clearing frost as it should. That's a part fault worth getting looked at. I can hear an occasional ticking/scraping sound from the back panel of the fridge. There's a bit of frost around the vent at the top back. No burning smell or anything tripping, thankfully. Should I go ahead with the full defrost?

Yes, go ahead with the full defrost. The ticking or scraping from the back panel, together with frost at the top-back vent, is the classic pattern for 22E: the fan blades are catching on ice, so the board sees the fan stalling. 1. Give it the full time, about 24 hours unplugged with the doors open. If you cut it short, ice behind the panel can survive and the fan will jam again within a day or two.
2. Once the ice has melted, look at the bottom of the back wall inside for the small defrost drain hole or channel. Gently flush it with warm water using a turkey baster or squeezy bottle, or use a soft pipe cleaner, nothing sharp. If water sits there instead of draining away, a blocked drain may be why the ice built up in the first place.
3. Dry it inside, plug it back in, and let it run with the doors shut for a few hours before reloading. Listen at the back panel: smooth whirring with no ticking is a good sign. - If the scraping has gone, 22E clears and it stays fine for a few weeks, it was most likely a one-off ice-up, perhaps from a door left ajar or a lot of warm food going in.
• If 22E or the scraping comes back within days to a couple of weeks, the automatic defrost probably isn't clearing frost as it should. That points to the defrost heater, its sensor, or the drain, and needs the internal panel off, so it's engineer territory.
• If it ticks or stays silent even with no ice, the fan motor itself becomes the main suspect. Let me know how it behaves once it's been running again.
Ok, I'll do the full defrost over the next day or so and report back. Will the freezer side be ok in the meantime if I leave the doors open on both sides? I have a cool box for the food.

Yes, leaving both doors open is fine, and it's actually the best way to do it. Unplugging switches off both sides anyway, so the freezer will warm up whatever you do. Opening its door too lets any frost in there melt at the same time, so the whole appliance starts fresh. It won't do the freezer any harm. 1. Food. Frozen food keeps best packed tightly together in the cool box with ice packs, lid kept shut. A full day is a long time for most cool boxes, so it's worth checking it now and then. Anything that has started to thaw but still has ice crystals in it can go back in the freezer. Anything fully thawed is best cooked or eaten soon rather than refrozen. Keep chilled items like meat, fish and dairy as cold as you can, and don't risk anything that has sat warm for hours.
2. Meltwater. The freezer side will drip too, so put towels in the bottom of both compartments and on the floor in front. Change them as they soak through.
3. Ice maker or dispenser. 4. Restarting. When you switch back on, give it a few hours with the doors shut. Let the freezer get properly cold before the frozen food goes back in. Then let me know whether 22E has cleared and whether the ticking from the back panel has gone. That will tell us whether this was a one-off ice-up, or whether the defrost system or the fan needs a closer look.
Great, thanks. I'll do the full defrost now and let you know whether 22E comes back.

Sounds like a plan. Once it's back on and has had a few hours to cool, these are the things worth noting for me: 1. Whether 22E has cleared from the display.
2. Whether the back panel sounds different: a smooth, steady whirr is good, while ticking or scraping means ice is still catching the fan (or the fan itself is struggling).
3. With the fridge door shut for a while, then opened, whether you can feel cool air coming from the top-back vent.
4. Over the next week or two, whether frost starts building around that vent again. If all four look good and stay that way, it was most likely a one-off ice-up. If the frost or the code creeps back, that points to the automatic defrost not doing its job, and we'll look at getting an engineer to check it. Let me know how it goes.
